## GBLUP and SNP-BLUP are the same answer in different coordinates

Traditional BLUP uses pedigree-based relationships. However, in GBLUP,
the mixed-model mechanism is retained, and pedigree relationships are
replaced with genomic relationships calculated from dense markers across
the genome.

Let's say two siblings have an expected pedigree relationship of 0.5, so
they share half of their alleles on average. In the genome, two siblings
might share 60% or 40% of their alleles, and dense markers directly
measure that deviation. GBLUP uses this concept, making the direct
relationship matrix a more accurate EBV.

With carefully matched parameters, GBLUP and SNP-BLUP yield identical
GEBVs, as both models imply the same covariance structure between
animals. This equivalence was documented by Habier et al. (2007),
VanRaden (2008), and Goddard (2009).

From a computational perspective, efficiency depends on the size of the
data being analysed. SNP-BLUP requires 50,000 matrix calculations
because it uses 50,000 SNP markers. GBLUP, on the other hand, regardless
of the number of markers, the efficiency of the matrix calculations
depends more on the size of the population/individuals being analysed.
Therefore, if we only have 1,000 individuals with 50,000 SNP markers,
the GBLUP model will certainly be more efficient. This is why GBLUP is
the preferred choice.

→ The mechanics of $\mathbf{G}$, the VanRaden constructions, and the
microhaplotype extension live in [GBLUP](blup-gblup.qmd). The full BLUP
family (PBLUP, GBLUP, GWABLUP) shares a single overview page at [Mixed
Model & BLUP Family](mixed-model-blup-family.qmd).

## Imputation is the cost lever, not just a data-cleaning step

After genotyping using SNP chips, some genotypes may be missing,
necessitating imputation. Imputation works by identifying the haplotypes
carried by each animal and matching them to animals with more dense
genotypes, then completing the missing genotypes from the matched
haplotypes. Softwares such as Beagle (Browning & Browning, 2007),
Fimpute (Sargolzaei et al., 2014), and Alphaimpute (Hickey et al., 2012)
work very well for imputation.

To optimise costs, breeding programs utilise genotype imputation. In
this strategy, a subset of key ancestors is subjected to high-density
genotyping to define the population's ancestral haplotypes. Their
descendants are then screened with affordable, low-density chips that
provide just enough markers to identify which specific high-density
segments were inherited. By reconstructing the missing high-density
genotypes using these ancestral templates, genomic analysis can proceed
as though every individual had been densely genotyped, providing
high-resolution genetic information at a significantly reduced cost.

→ See [Input Data → SNP](../input-data/snp.qmd) for the genotype
representations consumed by `masreml` and `masbayes`, including the demo
dataset where these constructions are applied.

## The Gaussian SNP-BLUP prior is a starting point, not the truth

SNP-BLUP (and implicitly GBLUP) assumes that every SNP has an effect
drawn from a normal distribution with the same variance. The estimate
for any one SNP then becomes a linear combination of all observed
phenotypes. Biologically, this equal-variance assumption is hard to
defend when real genetic architecture is sparser, with some SNPs near a
gene carrying an effect and many SNPs carrying none.

Methods in the Bayesian alphabet loosen this Gaussian prior in different
ways. The methods cited in the review fall into two families:

-   **Sparsity priors that mix "effect" with "no effect"**: BayesC
    (Habier et al., 2011, closest to SNP-BLUP), BayesB (Meuwissen et
    al., 2001, with a *t*-distribution for the effective SNPs), BayesR
    (Erbe et al., 2012, with a mixture of normals including one of large
    variance for big effects).
-   **Other shrinkage / sparsity estimators**: BayesA (Meuwissen et al.,
    2001), the LASSO, the Bayesian Lasso, and the elastic net (Hastie et
    al., 2009).

Many simulation studies showed that nonlinear methods (now machine
learning models) clearly outperforming GBLUP, but in real data, the gain
is trait-dependent, somewhat superior on some traits, not on others. So
often, simpler models with clear biological prior knowledge are more
preferred in genomic selection.

→ For the priors, MCMC and EM algorithms, and the BayesA/BayesR math
implemented in `masbayes`, see [Bayesian
Alphabet](bayesian-alphabet.qmd) and its sub-pages.
